title: Story of the First Sage of the Asylum
summary: Sultan Mohammed of Cairo, continuing his inspection of the city, visited the Moristan—the great hospital and sanctuary for the mentally afflicted.
full_text:
Sultan Mohammed of Cairo, continuing his inspection of the city, visited the Moristan—the great hospital and sanctuary for the mentally afflicted.

In one tranquil garden courtyard, he observed a dignified man with silver hair and luminous eyes, sitting beneath an orange tree and reading an ancient parchment.
Surprised by his composed demeanor, the Sultan approached and asked: 'Peace be upon thee, venerable sir. Why art thou confined in this house of the distracted?'

The man smiled with serene courtesy:
'O visitor, I am confined here because I suffer from an incurable illness called Truth-Telling.

In the bazaar and the imperial court, men flatter one another with false praise. They call cowards heroes, greedy thieves noble patrons, and fools sages, all to gain coppers and favor.
When I was a chief accountant in the treasury, I declared publicly that the grand chamberlain was pocketing public wheat. The chamberlain laughed, declared that only a raving lunatic would speak such inconvenient truths against powerful men, and had me placed in this peaceful hospital.

Here, within these quiet walls, no one lies to me. The madmen are honest about their delusions: one claims he is the moon, another that he is an earthenware pot. Neither pretends to love virtue while stealing from orphans.
Tell me, my noble guest: who is truly insane—the man who speaks truth and enjoys contentment under an orange tree, or the men in silk robes who betray their conscience every hour for fleeting dust?'

The Sultan stood transfixed by the philosopher's penetrating insight. He realized that society often labels those who refuse to participate in deceit as madmen.
He ordered the sage released with highest honors and appointed him Royal Censor of Truth, learning that genuine wisdom is often banished where falsehood reigns.
moral: Apparent eccentricity often conceals profound philosophical clarity; judge no man by outward appearances.
